PAPER: JHSMR Original Article Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Isosativan from the Nigerian Propolis Activates the mTORC2/AKT Pathway and Suppresses Muscle Atrophy Genes Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 in Diabetic Rats Mustafa Ibrahim Oladayo, Ph.D.1, Jimoh Lukman, M.Sc.2, Imam Abubakar Lekan, Ph.D.3, Ahmmed Bayo Opalekunde, Ph.D.4 1Department of Physiology, Faculty of Basic Medical Science, Federal University Oye-Ekiti, Ekiti State, Nigeria. 2Department of Physiology, Faculty of Basic Medical Science, Ahmadu Bello University Zaria, Zaria, Kaduna State, Nigeria. 3Department of Anatomy, Faculty of Basic Medical Science, University of Ilorin, Ilorin, Kwara State, Nigeria. 4Department of Medical Laboratory Science, Faculty of Medicine, Kwara State University, Malete, Kwara State, Nigeria. Received 14 December 2024 l Accepted 4 January 2025 l Published online 30 April 2025 Abstract: Objective: The study investigated the effects of Isosativan on the mTORC2/AKT pathway and diabetic muscle atrophy in a rat model of the disease. Material and Methods: Diabetes was induced by a high-fat diet and administration of a low-dose streptozotocin injection. The animals confirmed to be diabetic were subsequently treated with Isosativan (50 mg/kg) and their responses were evaluated based on muscle atrophy and body weight. Key biochemical pathways were assessed, particularly the mTORC2/ AKT signaling pathway and the muscle atrophy genes Atrogin-1 and MuRF1, in order to determine the mechanism underlying the effects of this Isosativan. Results: Administration of Isosativan resulted in significant improvements in diabetic muscle atrophy. The treated rats exhibited increased levels of the mTORC2 and AKT proteins and maintained relatively higher body weights compared to untreated diabetic controls. The muscle atrophy-related genes, Atrogin-1 and MuRF1, were also significantly suppressed in the treated group. Conclusion: Isosativan shows promise as a therapeutic agent for combating diabetes and diabetic muscle atrophy, operating through the activation of the mTORC2/AKT pathway, thereby leading to better utilization of glucose. This finding suggests that Isosativan could be a viable treatment option for managing diabetes-related metabolic problems, offering a novel approach for therapeutic intervention in diabetic muscle atrophy. JSON: Name: isosativan_mtorc2_aktdat_diabetic_muscle Title: Oral isosativan treatment and molecular signaling analysis to activate the mTORC2/AKT pathway for prevention of diabetic skeletal muscle atrophy in a high-fat diet/streptozotocin rat model Short Hypothesis: Oral administration of isosativan (50 mg/kg) activates mTORC2, increases AKT phosphorylation, and thereby reduces Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 expression to preserve skeletal muscle mass in HFD+STZ diabetic rats. Related Work: Natural propolis extracts and isolated flavonoids have been reported to modulate glucose metabolism, reduce inflammation, and affect mTOR/AMPK signaling; mTORC2 is established as an upstream activator of AKT that promotes muscle protein synthesis and suppresses atrophy, while Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 are validated markers/effectors of muscle proteolysis in catabolic and diabetic states. Existing studies are limited by use of crude propolis extracts rather than single isolated compounds, sparse in vivo mechanistic data linking specific propolis constituents to mTORC2 activation, inconsistent control of insulin signaling confounds, limited dose–response characterization, and incomplete functional muscle outcome measures (most focus on biochemical or in vitro endpoints). No prior work has comprehensively combined purified isosativan, dose-response, pharmacokinetics, pathway-specific inhibition, functional muscle testing, and standardized diabetic animal models to establish causality. Abstract: Diabetic skeletal muscle atrophy impairs function and metabolic control; targeted activation of mTORC2/AKT signaling may prevent atrophy by increasing protein synthesis and suppressing ubiquitin ligases Atrogin-1 and MuRF1. We propose a preclinical pipeline to evaluate purified isosativan, a flavonoid isolated from Nigerian propolis, as a molecular activator of mTORC2 in a high-fat diet plus low-dose streptozotocin (HFD+STZ) rat model of type 2 diabetes. The study will administer graded oral doses of purified isosativan and include pharmacokinetic profiling, pathway-specific inhibition (AKT inhibitor), and standard-of-care comparator (metformin). Primary readouts are gastrocnemius mass, muscle fiber cross-sectional area, grip strength, and molecular endpoints (mTORC2 abundance, p-AKT, p-4E-BP1, p-S6K1, PIP3, GLUT4 translocation, Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 mRNA/protein). Expected contributions are (1) demonstration of isosativan’s ability to activate mTORC2/AKT in vivo, (2) causal linkage between that activation and reduced muscle atrophy, and (3) quantitative dose–response and insulin-dependence data to support further translational evaluation. Experiments: Animal cohorts and sample sizes: male Wistar rats aged 8 weeks, n=12 per group (power calculation target: 80% power to detect 15% difference in gastrocnemius mass at alpha=0.05). Groups: (A) non-diabetic control (vehicle), (B) diabetic untreated (HFD+STZ + vehicle), (C) diabetic + metformin (250 mg/kg/day oral), (D) diabetic + isosativan low (25 mg/kg/day oral), (E) diabetic + isosativan mid (50 mg/kg/day oral), (F) diabetic + isosativan high (100 mg/kg/day oral), (G) diabetic + isosativan (50 mg/kg) + AKT inhibitor (MK-2206 at established dose), (H) diabetic + vehicle for inhibitor control. Diabetes induction: 8-week high-fat diet then single low-dose STZ (35 mg/kg i.p.); confirm diabetes by fasting glucose > 11.1 mmol/L on 2 consecutive measures. Isosativan: HPLC-purified, >95% purity; administer daily by oral gavage for 4 weeks post-diabetes confirmation. Endpoints and timepoints: baseline, weekly fasting blood glucose and weight, 4-week terminal tissue collection. Primary outcome measures: gastrocnemius wet weight normalized to tibia length; muscle fiber cross-sectional area (CSA) by histology (minimum 200 fibers per sample); forelimb grip strength (three trials averaged). Molecular assays: ELISA/Western blot quantification of mTORC2 complex (rictor/mTOR), p-AKT (Ser473), total AKT, p-4E-BP1, p-S6K1, GLUT4 subcellular fractionation for membrane translocation; PIP3 quantification by ELISA; qPCR for Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 normalized to GAPDH; measure plasma isosativan PK (Cmax, Tmax, AUC) at first dose and steady state. Metabolic tests: glucose tolerance test (GTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT) in week 3. Baselines: compare to non-diabetic control and metformin groups. Ablation/comparison studies: AKT inhibitor group tests necessity of AKT for isosativan effect; dose-response groups test sufficiency and potency. Data analysis: ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for multi-group comparisons; repeated-measures ANOVA for longitudinal glucose/weight; Cohen's d effect sizes; significance threshold p<0.05. Preprocessing and normalization: Western blots normalized to total protein and housekeeping control; qPCR using 2^-ΔΔCt with validated primers. Blinding and randomization: randomized group assignment and blinded outcome assessment for histology and molecular quantification. Risk Factors and Limitations: Compound-related: variable purity or stability of isolated isosativan, oral bioavailability and first-pass metabolism may limit systemic exposure; unknown off-target pharmacology causing confounding phenotypes. Model-related: HFD+STZ model variability in diabetes severity and muscle wasting; results limited to male Wistar rats and may not generalize across sex, strains, or human disease heterogeneity. Mechanistic ambiguity: incomplete separation of insulin-dependent versus insulin-independent effects if insulin signaling is not fully inhibited; compensatory pathways (AMPK, autophagy, inflammatory signaling) may mediate effects and confound interpretation. Measurement and assay limitations: antibody specificity for mTORC2 components and p-AKT may produce inconsistent quantification; PIP3 assays have limited dynamic range. Statistical and sample-size risks: animal-to-animal variability may reduce power for functional endpoints; multiple comparisons increase false-positive risk if not properly controlled. Translational limits: short-term (4-week) endpoints do not assess chronic safety, muscle function over longer durations, or human pharmacokinetics/toxicity. Regulatory and ethical constraints may limit escalating doses or chronic dosing required for translational studies.
